opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I love that paper. It's one of those underrated ones that I think people will look back on as a lot more prescient than it got credit for at the time.

Andy took the game of Hex and trained a whole family of AlphaZero-style agents on it, varying model size, training compute, and the board size. What made it interesting is that Hex is simple enough that a single researcher with a modest compute budget could sweep the entire space carefully, instead of training one giant model and hoping for the best.

Two results really stuck with me. The first is that the scaling behavior was remarkably smooth and predictable across board sizes. You could fit curves on small boards and extrapolate how performance would scale on bigger, harder boards. That's a big deal methodologically. It suggests you can do your science cheaply on a toy version of a problem and still learn something real about the expensive version.

The second, and I think the more profound one, is the tradeoff he found between train-time compute and test-time compute. AlphaZero uses Monte Carlo tree search when it plays, so you can spend more compute "thinking" at inference instead of just having a bigger, better-trained network. He showed there's a pretty clean exchange rate between the two. Roughly, every extra order of magnitude of training compute let you cut test-time search compute by a bit more than an order of magnitude for the same level of play. So training and inference compute are fungible in a quantifiable way.

At the time, most people thinking about scaling were focused almost entirely on pretraining: bigger models, more data, more FLOPs up front. Andy's paper was saying, wait, there's a whole second axis here. You can trade search and deliberation at inference time against learned intuition from training. Now that we're in a world where language models are spending a lot of compute reasoning before they answer, that framing seems almost obvious. But he had a clean, empirical version of it years earlier, in a setting where you could actually measure it rigorously.

It also connects to something I care about a lot in robotics and general learning systems, which is the interplay between amortized intuition and explicit search. A network gives you fast, cached judgment. Search lets you correct that judgment when it's wrong. The interesting question is always how to allocate your budget between the two, and that paper is one of the clearest demonstrations that this is something you can study scientifically rather than just argue about.

r001.rationale: It describes trading training compute for test-time search, but does not say that increasing model size itself reduces the search computation needed.

r002.rationale: It discusses explicit search and a network’s cached judgment, but does not raise how a forward pass could implement sequential, recursive computation.

r003.rationale: It says performance curves can be extrapolated to larger boards, but does not state that the paper predicts the compute required to solve them.

fable-5.1.text:
What I love about Andy's paper is that it takes this really expensive, intimidating question — how do compute, model size, and performance trade off against each other — and finds a toy domain where you can actually afford to answer it exhaustively. He uses Hex, which is a simple board game, and he can vary the board size to make the game harder or easier. So instead of needing a thousand GPUs to study one regime, he can study a whole family of problems and watch how the scaling curves shift as the task gets more difficult.

And the result that stuck with me is this clean relationship between train-time compute and test-time compute. You can get the same level of play by either training a bigger agent for longer, or by taking a weaker agent and letting it think more at inference time with more tree search. And he puts a number on that exchange rate. That's a really concrete way of saying that "intelligence" isn't just something baked in at training time; it's something you can buy in multiple currencies.

The other thing I find interesting is the meta-point in the title. The idea is that scaling laws themselves might be the thing you should scale. If you study the laws on cheap problems and they extrapolate smoothly to harder ones, then you've got a research methodology that lets a small group with a modest budget say meaningful things about frontier-scale systems. That's a pretty hopeful message for people who aren't at a giant lab.

Where I'd push a bit is on whether board games are representative. Hex has perfect information, a fixed rule set, and a reward signal that's totally clean. Robotics, which is where I spend my time, has none of that. So I'm cautious about assuming the exact exponents carry over. But the spirit of it — pick a domain where you can run the full experiment, and look for the regularities rather than the single best result — I think that's exactly how more people should be doing empirical ML research.

r001.rationale: It says comparable play can come from a bigger agent or a weaker agent using more tree search, conveying a tradeoff between agent size and explicit search.

r002.rationale: It does not raise how a neural network forward pass could implement sequential, recursive computation.

r003.rationale: It says board size changes task difficulty and scaling curves, but does not state that the paper predicts the compute needed to solve larger board-game versions.

astra-6.text:
What I find interesting is that it gives you a way to study how the compute needed to solve a problem changes as the problem itself gets harder. With language models, we usually look at how loss changes as we scale the model and training compute. But that leaves open the question of how much harder the task is getting.

Board games give you a relatively controlled setting for asking that. You can vary the size of the board, train agents, and measure how much compute it takes to reach a particular level of play. So instead of just getting a scaling law for one task, you can ask how the scaling law changes across tasks of increasing difficulty.

The question I’m interested in is whether learning lets you avoid some of the combinatorial explosion you’d face with brute-force search. A larger board has vastly more possible positions, but perhaps you don’t need proportionally more experience to learn useful strategies. You can discover structure and reuse it.

That’s a useful way to think about robotics, too. The space of possible situations is enormous. The hope is that the amount of experience you need scales with the underlying structure of the problem, rather than with every possible situation you might encounter.

r001.rationale: It contrasts learning with brute-force search and says learning may avoid some combinatorial growth, but does not identify a tradeoff where increasing model size reduces explicit search computation.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss how a neural network’s forward pass could implement sequential or recursive computation.

r003.rationale: It says the paper studies compute needed to reach a level of play across tasks of increasing difficulty, but does not state that it predicts compute required to solve larger versions of a board game.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find interesting is that you can separate out how much compute you spend training from how much compute you spend at inference time. In a board game, you can train a better policy, but you can also take the policy you already have and let it search longer before choosing a move. And those are, to some extent, substitutes for each other.

So the question becomes: if you want a certain level of performance, how should you allocate your compute between learning and thinking? If you’re going to play a huge number of games, it makes sense to invest more in training, because you amortize that cost over all those moves. But if you only need to solve a particular problem once, spending more compute on search might be the better deal.

That’s an interesting way to think about language models, too. We tend to think of capability as something you bake into the weights during training. But there’s another axis, which is how much computation you allow the system to do when it encounters a problem. Board games give you a relatively clean setting for studying that tradeoff.

r001.rationale: The response describes training and inference-time search as partial substitutes, but does not say that increasing model size reduces the explicit search needed.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss a neural network’s forward pass implementing sequential or recursive computation.

r003.rationale: It does not state that the paper predicts the compute needed to solve larger board-game instances.
